title: The Future of Employment: How Susceptible Are Jobs to Computerisation?
pub: Technological Forecasting and Social Change, vol. 114, pp. 254-280 (January 2017), DOI 10.1016/j.techfore.2016.08.019; OA version: Oxford Martin School working paper (September 17, 2013)
author: Carl Benedikt Frey · Michael A. Osborne

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Employment effects: Task substitution permits stable jobs
st.an: The source accepts task-level substitution and worker reallocation rather than treating technical exposure as automatic aggregate job loss. It materially extends the cluster by replacing the routine/non-routine boundary with engineering bottlenecks and data availability, while making reallocation conditional on falling computing costs, relative wages and comparative advantage.
qs: Our model thus predicts that the pace at which these bottlenecks can be overcome will determine the extent of computerisation in the twenty-first cen- tury.

With expanding computa- tional capabilities, resulting from technological advances, and a falling market price of computing, workers in susceptible tasks will thus reallocate to non- susceptible tasks.

st.t: Exposure rankings: Different measures reorder legal work
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition by presenting computerisation probabilities as occupation-specific susceptibility estimates and showing sharp variation within legal work, especially between lawyers and legal support roles. Because it provides neither observed job-loss data nor staffing recommendations, it does not justify treating these probabilities as direct displacement measures.

st.t: Job exposure: Which tasks vanish changes outcomes
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central distinction between technological exposure and occupational disappearance. It estimates potential automatability rather than realised job losses, recognises task reallocation and productivity effects as omitted mechanisms, and illustrates how automation may affect legal tasks and occupations differently.
qs: We make no attempt to estimate the number of jobs that will actually be automated, and focus on potential job automatability over some unspecified number of years.
do not capture any within-occupation variation resulting from the computerisa- tion of tasks that simply free-up time for human labour to perform other tasks.

st.t: Legal occupations: Susceptibility measures resist direct comparison
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition by showing large occupation-specific differences in computerisation probabilities, including between lawyers and legal support roles. As a probability table without supplied evidence of observed job losses or generative-AI exposure, it supports comparative susceptibility analysis rather than direct displacement forecasts or comparison with differently defined measures.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s task-reconfiguration framing by distinguishing automatable legal writing from less susceptible persuasion and by predicting substitution across tasks rather than demonstrated profession-wide displacement. Its explicit limitation to technological susceptibility and substitution, not net employment change, also aligns with the cluster’s caution against treating exposure as realised job loss, although it does not address verification or apprenticeship risks.
qs: In the present study, we will argue that legal writing and truck driving will soon be automated, while persuading, for instance, will not.
Our analysis is thus limited to the substitution effect of future computerisation.

st.t: Task change: Small job effects can widen inequality
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s qualified distinction between technological exposure and realised job loss, and its finding that education and wages correlate with lower predicted susceptibility. Its contribution is predictive rather than evidence of actual displacement or widening inequality, so it supports only part of the broader synthesis.
qs: Figure IV reveals that both wages and educational attainment exhibit a strong negative relation- ship with the probability of computerisation.
We make no attempt to estimate how many jobs will actually be automated.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core task-level framing: automation susceptibility varies with specific engineering bottlenecks, work can be restructured around those constraints, and automating some tasks may reallocate rather than eliminate human work. It also cautions that technical automatability is not a forecast of realised job losses. However, it does not address the cluster’s legal-AI-specific emphasis on user expertise, verification or operating-model implementation.
qs: The extent of computerisation in the twenty-first century will thus partly depend on innovative approaches to task restructuring.

Of course, many occupations being affected by these developments are still far from fully computerisable, meaning that the computerisation of some tasks will simply free-up time for human labour to perform other tasks.

kp.k: Computerisation potentially extends beyond routine work
kp.d: Frey and Osborne argue that machine learning, big data and mobile robotics expand automation into non-routine cognitive and manual tasks. Their forward-looking framework replaces a simple routine/non-routine distinction with an assessment of remaining engineering bottlenecks. They explicitly predict automation of legal writing and truck driving, while treating persuasion as substantially more resistant.
qs: In the present study, we will argue that legal writing and truck driving will soon be automated, while persuading, for instance, will not.
The extent of computerisation in the twenty-first century will thus partly depend on innovative approaches to task restructuring.

kp.k: Three engineering bottlenecks underpin occupational susceptibility
kp.d: The authors identify perception and manipulation, creative intelligence, and social intelligence as obstacles to substitution. Unstructured environments, irregular objects and failure recovery challenge robotics; specifying creative value challenges computational creativity; negotiation, persuasion and care require social understanding. These are assessments of technological capabilities made in the September 17, 2013 working paper, not observations of subsequent AI performance.
qs: Human social intelligence is important in a wide range of work tasks, such as those involving negotiation, persuasion and care.
In the absence of engineering solutions to overcome this problem, it seems unlikely that occupations requiring a high degree of creative intelligence will be automated in the next decades.

kp.k: Estimates combine expert labels and occupational characteristics
kp.d: The study links 2010 O*NET occupational characteristics to 2010 BLS employment and wage data, producing 702 occupations covering 138.44 million jobs and excluding 4.628 million jobs, or 3 percent of total employment. Researchers hand-labelled 70 occupations and trained a Gaussian process classifier using nine variables representing the three bottlenecks. Positive labels required all occupational tasks to be considered automatable, allowing for task simplification; labels were restricted to occupations about which researchers were most confident.
qs: Thus, we only assigned a 1 to fully automatable occupations, where we considered all tasks to be automatable.
Labels were assigned only to the occupations about which we were most confident.
We note that US employment for the 702 occupations we considered is 138.44 million.

kp.k: Validation tests agreement with researchers’ labels
kp.d: The authors repeatedly split the 70 labelled occupations into equal training and test halves, averaging results across 100 random selections. The exponentiated quadratic Gaussian process achieved AUC 0.894 and log-likelihood −163.3, compared with 0.827 and −205.0 for the linear model. This tests consistency between expert labels and occupational variables, rather than observed future automation; the authors explicitly treat their hand labels as noisy and uncertain.
qs: This means that our algorithm verified that our subjective judgements were systematically and consistently related to the O∗NET variables.
We thus acknowledge that it is by no means certain that a job is computerisable given our labelling.

kp.k: Forty-seven percent denotes potential exposure, not predicted job losses
kp.d: Using probability thresholds of 0.3 and 0.7, the study places approximately 33 percent of employment in low-risk occupations, 19 percent in medium-risk occupations and 47 percent in high-risk occupations. These estimates concern the mix of jobs existing in 2010. The suggested horizon is unspecified, perhaps a decade or two from the paper’s perspective; the authors expressly do not estimate actual automation or future net employment.
qs: We make no attempt to estimate how many jobs will actually be automated.
We therefore focus on the impact of computerisation on the mix of jobs that existed in 2010.
We refer to these as jobs at risk – i.e. jobs we expect could be automated relatively soon, perhaps over the next decade or two.

kp.k: Legal research software already changes document-intensive work
kp.d: Drawing on Markoff (2011), the authors report that algorithms are taking on tasks performed by paralegals and contract and patent lawyers. They describe law firms using computers to scan briefs and precedents for pre-trial research, citing Symantec’s Clearwell system as capable of analysing and sorting more than 570,000 documents in two days. This is a reported example of task automation and assistance, not the study’s own measurement of legal employment losses.
qs: More specifically, law firms now rely on computers that can scan thousands of legal briefs and precedents to assist in pre-trial research.
proved capable of analysing and sorting more than 570,000 documents in two days (Markoff, 2011).

kp.k: Lawyers and legal support receive sharply different estimates
kp.d: The appendix assigns lawyers a computerisation probability of 0.035, paralegals and legal assistants 0.94, legal secretaries 0.98, and title examiners, abstractors, and searchers 0.99. Lawyers were hand-labelled non-computerisable and paralegals and legal assistants computerisable. The authors explain the contrast through lawyers’ creative and social intelligence requirements and predict that automated legal research will complement lawyers in the medium term. These probabilities concern full occupational automation, not the fraction of tasks or workers displaced.
qs: At the same time, lawyers, which rely on labour input from legal assistants, are in the low risk category.

Thus, for the work of lawyers to be fully automated, engineering bottlenecks to creative and social intelligence will need to be overcome, implying that the computerisation of legal research will complement the work of lawyers in the medium term.

kp.k: Automation can assist judgment without fully replacing decision-makers
kp.d: The authors distinguish applications where algorithmic recommendations inform human operators from those where algorithms make decisions directly. They argue that scalability, pattern detection and the absence of some human biases advantage computers. Their discussion cites Danziger et al. (2011) on Israeli judges’ greater generosity after lunch breaks as motivation for algorithmic assistance; it does not establish that algorithmic legal decisions are unbiased or superior through a direct comparative test.
qs: It can thus be argued that many roles involving decision-making will benefit from impartial algorithmic solutions.

Of course, many occupations being affected by these developments are still far from fully computerisable, meaning that the computerisation of some tasks will simply free-up time for human labour to perform other tasks.

kp.k: Automation may advance in waves separated by bottlenecks
kp.d: The authors interpret their estimates as suggesting an initial wave affecting transportation and logistics, office and administrative support, production, and substantial portions of services, sales and construction. A subsequent slowdown would reflect persistent engineering barriers. Medium-risk work depends particularly on progress in perception and manipulation; further substitution in low-risk occupations would require overcoming creative and social intelligence bottlenecks. This is a technological scenario rather than a dated adoption forecast.
qs: Seen from this perspective, our findings could be interpreted as two waves of computerisation, separated by a “technological plateau”.
More specifically, the computerisation of occupations in the medium risk category will mainly depend on perception and manipulation challenges.

kp.k: Lower wages and education correlate with greater susceptibility
kp.d: Across the study’s occupational estimates, wages and the share of workers with a bachelor’s degree or higher are negatively associated with computerisation probability. The authors predict a break from historical labour-market polarisation: rather than predominantly hollowing out middle-income work, prospective automation would concentrate on low-skill, low-wage occupations. They recommend acquisition of creative and social skills as workers move toward less susceptible tasks.
qs: Figure IV reveals that both wages and educational attainment exhibit a strong negative relationship with the probability of computerisation.
For workers to win the race, however, they will have to acquire creative and social skills.

kp.k: Historical mechanisms distinguish displacement from net employment outcomes
kp.d: The historical review contrasts nineteenth-century deskilling, twentieth-century capital–skill complementarity and computer-era polarisation. The authors explain that labour-saving innovations can destroy existing work while lower prices, higher real incomes and industry entry create demand elsewhere. They acknowledge that the employment-expanding effect has predominated historically, but their own estimates address only substitution and do not calculate countervailing job creation.
qs: Hence, in short, technological progress has two competing effects on employment (Aghion and Howitt, 1994).
Our analysis is thus limited to the substitution effect of future computerisation.

kp.k: Adoption economics, regulation and task variation limit predictions
kp.d: The study does not incorporate future wage levels, capital prices or labour shortages, which can affect adoption incentives and timing. Regulatory change, political resistance and public acceptance may also slow implementation. The authors avoid estimating when engineering bottlenecks will be overcome, and their full-occupation probabilities do not capture within-occupation task reallocation or the employment consequences of productivity gains.
qs: Second, regulatory concerns and political activism may slow down the process of computerisation.
We avoid making predictions about the legislatory process and the public acceptance of technological progress, and thus the pace of computerisation.
Although it is clear that the impact of productivity gains on employment will vary across occupations and industries, we make no attempt to examine such effects.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Frey and Osborne predict automation of legal writing and research tasks, while distinguishing substitution for legal support workers from medium-term augmentation of lawyers.
pts.d: The authors argue that legal writing will soon be automated and report that algorithms are already taking on tasks performed by paralegals and contract and patent lawyers. Their occupational model places paralegals and legal assistants in the high-risk category and lawyers in the low-risk category. They explain that full automation of lawyers depends on overcoming creative- and social-intelligence bottlenecks; meanwhile, computerised legal research complements lawyers. The claim about automating legal writing is therefore distinct from a claim that the entire lawyer occupation will disappear.

pts.k: Across the US labour market, the authors estimate that approximately 47 percent of employment is in occupations highly susceptible to computerisation.
pts.d: This cross-domain paper examines computerisation through machine learning and mobile robotics, rather than contemporary generative AI alone. It predicts exposure extending beyond routine work into non-routine cognitive and manual tasks. Transportation and logistics, office and administrative support, and production are prominent high-risk groups, alongside substantial employment in services, sales and construction. The authors describe an initial automation wave followed by a technological plateau, with further substitution dependent on overcoming engineering bottlenecks. Their model associates higher wages and educational attainment with lower susceptibility and predicts that future substitution will principally affect low-skill, low-wage work rather than continue the previous pattern of middle-income hollowing-out.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The occupational estimates combine expert judgements, occupational characteristics and a Gaussian process classifier; the legal-task discussion also cites a reported document-processing example.
pts.d: Frey and Osborne combine 2010 O*NET occupational information with 2010 BLS employment and wage data for 702 occupations. They and machine-learning researchers hand-labelled 70 occupations, assigning the automatable label only where they considered all tasks automatable, while allowing for task simplification and the availability of big data. Nine occupational variables proxy perception and manipulation, creative intelligence and social intelligence. A Gaussian process classifier extrapolates from those labels. Repeated random half-training/half-test splits produced an AUC of 0.894 for the selected classifier: this measures reproduction of expert labels, not observed future automation. For legal services, the authors cite Markoff (2011) on Symantec's Clearwell system analysing and sorting more than 570,000 documents in two days. That is a cited operational example, not an original legal-quality or employment-impact experiment.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The estimates concern potential full-occupation automation over an unspecified horizon, tentatively a decade or two, rather than actual job losses by a fixed deadline.
pts.d: The supplied body is dated September 17, 2013, notwithstanding the bibliographic reference to journal publication in 2017; its relative timeframes should be read from that working-paper context. The authors describe high-risk jobs as potentially automatable relatively soon, perhaps within a decade or two, and legal-research complementarity as medium-term. Progress depends on sufficient data, specification or restructuring of tasks, and resolution of perception/manipulation, creative-intelligence and social-intelligence bottlenecks. They do not predict when those bottlenecks will be overcome. Adoption also depends on wages, capital costs, labour availability, regulation, political resistance and public acceptance. They explicitly do not estimate actual automation, net employment changes, productivity-driven job creation or within-occupation time savings. Their analysis applies to the 2010 occupational employment mix.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The legal-sector estimates vary sharply by occupation; support and document-search roles receive much higher susceptibility estimates than lawyers and mediators.
pts.d: The appendix assigns model probabilities of 0.035 to lawyers, 0.06 to arbitrators, mediators and conciliators, 0.40 to judges, magistrate judges and magistrates, 0.41 to judicial law clerks, 0.46 to court, municipal and license clerks, 0.50 to court reporters, and 0.64 to administrative law judges, adjudicators and hearing officers. Higher estimates include 0.94 for paralegals and legal assistants, 0.98 for legal secretaries, and 0.99 for title examiners, abstractors and searchers. These are probabilities assigned to occupational automatability, not percentages of workers predicted to lose jobs or shares of tasks automated. Law firms are described as users of research automation, while lawyers benefit from complementary research inputs even as legal support work faces substitution. The source does not segment effects by firm size, partner or associate seniority, client type or legal-market business model. Across the broader economy, the authors identify low-skill workers as needing to acquire creative and social skills.
